about: © 2026 RADAF. All rights reserved. CAPS-DI pedagogical knowledge base. CAPS says WHAT must be learned; these rules say HOW it is taught; learner data decides how teaching is adapted. Items marked origin=roadmap come from the CAPS-DI pedagogical roadmap; origin=author were added by the CAPS-DI author; origin=added are common Foundation Phase errors added for coverage and should be reviewed. origin=research items are paraphrased from published South African reading research listed in sources.

barriers.name: Prerequisite gap
barriers.description: The learner does not know the skill yet.

barriers.name: Misconception
barriers.description: The learner has learned something incorrectly.

barriers.name: Access barrier
barriers.description: The learner may know the concept but cannot show it through the current mode of instruction.

barriers.name: Processing barrier
barriers.description: The learner needs more processing time, repetition or reduced cognitive load.

barriers.name: Language barrier
barriers.description: The learner understands the concept but lacks the vocabulary or English to express it.

barriers.name: Attention / regulation barrier
barriers.description: The learner cannot sustain engagement with the current instructional format.

barriers.name: Motor / transcription barrier
barriers.description: The learner knows what to write but handwriting limits output.

barriers.name: Insufficient challenge
barriers.description: The learner has already mastered the target and needs greater complexity.

dimensions.access: How learners take in the content: visuals, oral explanation, concrete materials, movement, audio, enlarged print, vocabulary pre-teaching.
dimensions.process: How learners work with the concept: extra modelling, reduced cognitive load, guided practice, repetition, structured partner work, manipulatives.
dimensions.support: Temporary scaffolds: prompts, cues, sentence frames, word banks, graphic organisers, worked examples, checklists.
dimensions.response: How learners show understanding: oral response, pointing, drawing, selecting, constructing, writing, reading aloud.
dimensions.challenge: How complexity rises for learners who have mastered the outcome: more complex text, independent application, explanation, justification, comparison, inference, creation.

phonics.name: Systematic explicit phonics
steps: Review letter-sound links (alphabetic principle)
Hear the sounds in the spoken word
Map each sound to its letter
Blend left to right and read the word
Then segment: break the word back into its sounds
Spell (encode) it, a letter for each sound
Apply in decodable text and dictation

phonological.name: Oral phonological awareness before print
steps: Listen for rhyme and syllables
Isolate the first sound
Blend sounds orally
Segment orally
Manipulate sounds
Link to letters

fluency.name: Modelled and repeated reading
steps: Teacher models fluent reading
Echo reading
Choral reading
Repeated meaningful rereading
Phrasing and expression practice
Independent rereading

comprehension.name: Explicit comprehension instruction
steps: Activate background knowledge before reading
Teach one strategy explicitly with NEMPA: Name it, Explain it, Model it with a think-aloud, Practise together, Apply independently
Strategies across the year: predicting, visualising, inferring, monitoring and repair (stop, reread, fix), summarising
Ask a mix of literal (in the text), inferential (text clues plus what you know) and evaluative (your opinion) questions
Learner explains the answer with evidence from the text
Independent application in group guided and paired reading

oral.name: Oral language and vocabulary development
steps: Choose 5–8 words of the week from the shared-reading text or theme
Introduce each word explicitly with a flash card, picture, action and a child-friendly meaning
Put the words on the word wall and revisit them every day across activities (read-aloud, phonics, writing, Life Skills, Maths)
Learners say, read and use each word in a sentence; extend learners’ answers with richer words
Read aloud daily from varied texts so learners meet words not used in everyday speech
Check: can learners use the words in speech and writing by the end of the week?

writing.name: Oral rehearsal to independent writing
steps: Talk about the idea
Plan (draw or list)
Teacher models writing
Shared and supported composition
Independent writing
Feedback and revision

handwriting.name: Multisensory letter formation
steps: Model formation with verbal path
Trace in sand or air
Trace on paper
Copy with starting dots
Write from memory
Write within words and sentences

letterKnowledge.name: Multisensory letter introduction
steps: Show the letter shape
Say its sound (and name)
Trace it in sand or the air
Find it in words and the environment
Daily cumulative review of all letters taught

phonemic.name: Oral phonemic awareness (no print)
steps: Listen for the first sound
Isolate sounds with counters or fingers
Blend sounds orally (/c/-/a/-/t/ → cat)
Segment spoken words into sounds
Swap a sound to make a new word
Then link the sounds to letters

segmenting.name: Segmenting for spelling (encoding)
steps: Say the word slowly
Tap or push a counter for each sound
Count the sounds
Write a letter for each sound in order
Check by blending back what was written
Apply in dictated words and short sentences

Term 1.question: Does the learner have the foundational knowledge and skills for this CAPS outcome?
Term 1.sequence: Explicit teaching, modelling, guided practice, repetition, multisensory practice, immediate feedback
Term 1.look_for: prerequisite gaps, foundational misconceptions, language barriers, phonological difficulties, vocabulary gaps, attention or participation barriers

Term 2.question: Can the learner use foundational skills to understand and communicate meaning?
Term 2.sequence: Model, guided practice, purposeful practice, feedback, application
Term 2.look_for: whether the difficulty is decoding or meaning (vocabulary, comprehension) — respond to the actual barrier, not with more of the same

Term 3.question: What is preventing this learner from accessing the same CAPS outcome?
Term 3.sequence: Diagnose the barrier from evidence, then adapt access, process, support, response or challenge
Term 3.look_for: the specific barrier type (prerequisite, misconception, access, processing, language, attention, motor, insufficient challenge)

Term 4.question: Can the learner apply the skill independently in a new context?
Term 4.sequence: Model, guide, prompt, fade, independent application, transfer
Term 4.look_for: self-correction, strategy choice, explaining thinking, applying the skill to unfamiliar texts and tasks, readiness for the next grade

misconceptions.misconception: Confuses visually similar letters
misconceptions.evidence: Reads or writes b for d, p for q
misconceptions.response: Multisensory formation with verbal path; one letter at a time; anchor picture or gesture for each

misconceptions.misconception: Does not yet recognise the taught letters
misconceptions.evidence: Cannot point to or name letters that have been taught
misconceptions.response: Multisensory letter introduction (shape, sound, formation) with daily cumulative review

misconceptions.misconception: Cannot link the letter's sound to its name
misconceptions.evidence: Knows the letter name but not its sound, or the sound but not which letter (name) it belongs to
misconceptions.response: Teach name, sound and shape together for each taught letter (say the name, say the sound, trace the shape); daily quick matching: show the letter and say name and sound, hear the sound and point to the letter

misconceptions.misconception: Knows the letters in order but not mixed up
misconceptions.evidence: Recites the alphabet or sound chart but cannot give the sounds when letters are shown out of order
misconceptions.response: Replace chanting with shuffled-card practice to individuals; return to missed cards after two or three others

misconceptions.misconception: Cannot separate the sounds in a word
misconceptions.evidence: Gives syllables instead of individual sounds
misconceptions.response: Oral phoneme segmentation before print (sound boxes, counters, tapping)

misconceptions.misconception: Cannot hear the first sound in a spoken word
misconceptions.evidence: Cannot say which of 'mat, sun, map' start the same way
misconceptions.response: Oral sound isolation games with no print: 'I spy something starting with /m/'; mouth-shape mirrors

misconceptions.misconception: Cannot blend sounds they hear
misconceptions.evidence: Teacher says /s/-/u/-/n/ and the learner cannot say 'sun'
misconceptions.response: Oral blending before print: stretch the sounds ('sssuuunnn'), robot talk, start with two sounds

misconceptions.misconception: Thinks the letter name is the sound
misconceptions.evidence: Says the letter name (e.g. 'em') instead of the sound /m/
misconceptions.response: Explicit sound discrimination and grapheme–phoneme mapping

misconceptions.misconception: Relies on memorised words instead of decoding
misconceptions.evidence: Reads familiar words but cannot read unfamiliar CVC words; reads familiar words but fails on made-up (nonsense) words
misconceptions.response: Hear, segment, map sounds to letters, blend, read, encode, apply in text

misconceptions.misconception: Reads a two-letter sound as two sounds
misconceptions.evidence: Reads sh as s-h, ch as c-h or th as t-h
misconceptions.response: Teach each digraph explicitly as one sound after its single letters, with plenty of word practice

misconceptions.misconception: Reads from the first letter only
misconceptions.evidence: Guesses words that start with the same sound
misconceptions.response: Segment every phoneme, then blend all the way through the word

misconceptions.misconception: Says each sound but cannot blend them into a word
misconceptions.evidence: Reads /c/ /a/ /t/ correctly but does not say 'cat'
misconceptions.response: Continuous blending: hold each sound into the next; start with stretchy sounds (m, s, a); successive blending (ca… cat)

misconceptions.misconception: Blends out of order
misconceptions.evidence: Reads 'tac' or 'act' for cat
misconceptions.response: Finger-track left to right; sweep under the word; sound boxes with arrows

misconceptions.misconception: Stalls on consonant blends
misconceptions.evidence: Knows each letter but gets stuck on st, bl, fr or similar blends
misconceptions.response: Show the blend as two known sounds said quickly together, then practise in words

misconceptions.misconception: Hears only the first sound of a word
misconceptions.evidence: Asked for the sounds in 'cat', says /c/ and stops; spells cat as 'c' or 'k'
misconceptions.response: Sound boxes with counters: push one counter per sound; stretch the word slowly ('mmmaaat')

misconceptions.misconception: Splits words into chunks, not single sounds
misconceptions.evidence: Says 'c – at' instead of /c/ /a/ /t/
misconceptions.response: Model one sound per finger or counter; contrast chunk vs sound; practise with two- then three-sound words

misconceptions.misconception: Hears the sounds but writes them in the wrong order
misconceptions.evidence: Writes 'tac' or 'cta' for cat
misconceptions.response: Say-tap-write: tap each sound left to right on the arm or sound boxes, then write each letter in that order; blend back to check

misconceptions.misconception: Guesses words from the pictures
misconceptions.evidence: Correct only when the picture supports the word
misconceptions.response: Cover picture cues; decode first, then confirm meaning with the picture

misconceptions.misconception: Reads word by word
misconceptions.evidence: Accurate but slow, laboured reading without phrasing
misconceptions.response: Model phrasing; repeated, meaningful rereading; echo and choral reading

misconceptions.misconception: Reads slowly and makes many errors
misconceptions.evidence: Many words read wrongly: in English fewer than about 85% correct (about 95% in an African home language)
misconceptions.response: Return to targeted phonics and word reading before fluency practice

misconceptions.misconception: Reads accurately but very slowly
misconceptions.evidence: Most words correct (English about 85% or more) but slow and effortful
misconceptions.response: Repeated reading (up to about four times) of slightly easy texts, plus wide reading; do not push for speed

misconceptions.misconception: Reads without expression or phrasing
misconceptions.evidence: Flat, word-by-word voice; ignores full stops and question marks
misconceptions.response: Model expressive reading; echo and choral reading; teach phrasing and punctuation cues

misconceptions.misconception: Retells isolated events
misconceptions.evidence: Cannot say what the story is mostly about
misconceptions.response: Sequencing with picture cards and modelling of the main idea

misconceptions.misconception: Answers literal but not inferential questions
misconceptions.evidence: Performance drops when the question asks why or what might happen
misconceptions.response: Explicit inference modelling and graduated questioning (literal to inferential)

misconceptions.misconception: Decodes accurately but does not attend to meaning
misconceptions.evidence: Reads the text correctly but cannot answer simple questions about it
misconceptions.response: Pre-teach key vocabulary; stop and talk about meaning; oral retell after each page

misconceptions.misconception: Gives answers not supported by the text
misconceptions.evidence: Cannot point to what in the text or picture shows the answer
misconceptions.response: Ask 'What makes you think that?'; model finding evidence

misconceptions.misconception: Follows only part of an instruction
misconceptions.evidence: Completes the first step of a two-step instruction only
misconceptions.response: Chunk instructions; visual cue cards; learner repeats the steps back before starting

misconceptions.misconception: Answers in single words
misconceptions.evidence: Gives one-word answers even when prompted for more
misconceptions.response: Model full-sentence answers; sentence frames; think-pair-share oral rehearsal

misconceptions.misconception: Retells events out of order
misconceptions.evidence: Mixes the beginning, middle and end when retelling
misconceptions.response: Picture sequencing cards; first, then, last frames; act out the story

misconceptions.misconception: Uses broad, general words
misconceptions.evidence: Says 'thing', 'nice', 'big' instead of precise words
misconceptions.response: Explicit vocabulary instruction with pictures and objects; build word webs

misconceptions.misconception: Writes ideas as disconnected sentences
misconceptions.evidence: Sentences do not link to one another
misconceptions.response: Oral rehearsal, sentence combining and sequencing

misconceptions.misconception: Does not mark sentence boundaries
misconceptions.evidence: Writing has no capital letters or full stops
misconceptions.response: Model and orally 'say the sentence'; capital-and-full-stop checklist; shared editing

misconceptions.misconception: Leaves out vowels when spelling
misconceptions.evidence: Writes 'ct' for cat, 'dg' for dog
misconceptions.response: Oral segmenting with sound boxes before writing; vowel focus with anchor pictures

misconceptions.misconception: Writes exactly as they speak
misconceptions.evidence: The same sentence errors recur in writing
misconceptions.response: Explicit sentence modelling and guided transformation

misconceptions.misconception: Knows the letter but forms it inconsistently
misconceptions.evidence: Letters start in the wrong place or vary in size
misconceptions.response: Multisensory formation practice and reduced copying load

misconceptions.misconception: Copies letter by letter from the board
misconceptions.evidence: Very slow copying, loses place, incomplete work
misconceptions.response: Copy from a card on the desk; copy whole words; reduce copying length

misconceptions.misconception: Has already mastered the outcome
misconceptions.evidence: Completes tasks quickly and accurately; disengages
misconceptions.response: Increase complexity: explain, justify, apply to a new text, create

misconceptions.misconception: Cannot sustain attention in long whole-class input
misconceptions.evidence: Off task after a few minutes; better in short, active tasks
misconceptions.response: 3–5 minute segments, movement breaks, active response (cards, gestures)

decoding.note: Decoding and encoding have five components, taught in this order: letter knowledge, phonemic awareness, alphabetic principle, blending, then segmenting. Diagnose which one breaks down; each needs a different response.

components.name: Letter knowledge
components.what: Recognises the shapes and names of letters and letter combinations

components.name: Phonemic awareness
components.what: Purely auditory: hears, isolates, blends, segments and swaps individual sounds in spoken words — no print

components.name: Alphabetic principle
components.what: Knows that letters (graphemes) map systematically to sounds (phonemes)

components.name: Blending
components.what: Says the sounds left to right and smooths them into a word (reading)

components.name: Segmenting
components.what: The reverse of blending: breaks a spoken word into all its separate sounds and writes a letter for each sound (spelling / encoding)

letterSounds.what: Letter-sound knowledge: 1-minute, one-to-one test, letters in random order, errors subtracted (as in EGRA)
letterSounds.target: 40 letters correct per minute by the end of Grade 1
letterSounds.when: Test near the end of Term 3 in Grade 1; use Term 4 to reteach the sounds learners still miss
letterSounds.why: South African studies found learners below about 40 letters per minute could not yet read words

accuracyBeforeSpeed.target: English (an opaque spelling system, and often a second language): about 85% of words correct signals developed accuracy. African home languages (transparent spelling): about 95%.
accuracyBeforeSpeed.source: EFAL benchmarking summary report (2022), p. 5; Module 3, p. 66

orfAfricanLanguages.what: Oral reading fluency (words correct per minute)
orfAfricanLanguages.note: Different because isiZulu writes long joined (conjunctive) words. For English as a First Additional Language see orfEFAL.

phonicsTime.target: About 15 minutes a day in Grades 1–3 (CAPS); in Grade 1 Term 1 about one new sound a week, then at least two a week

orfEFAL.what: English First Additional Language oral reading fluency, correct words per minute (cwpm), minimum by the END of each grade, grade-appropriate passage, one-to-one
orfEFAL.zones: Below 50 cwpm learners cannot yet understand what they read; 50–89 cwpm is a development zone (typically 4–6 of 10 questions right); from about 90 cwpm most questions are answered
orfEFAL.context: Set from data on over 20,000 learners in no-fee schools in 6 provinces. By the end of Grade 3, 19–34% of learners in these samples could not read one English word correctly, and only 19–37% reached 50 cwpm. About 90% of learners learn in English from Grade 4.
orfEFAL.appliesTo: Learners reading English as an additional language. There is no official South African benchmark for English Home Language; do not apply these as HL targets.
orfEFAL.source: Wills, Ardington, Pretorius & Sebaeng (2022), EFAL benchmarking summary report, pp. 4–14

phonicsLesson.note: Structure of an effective phonics lesson (about 15–20 minutes), in our own words
steps: Brisk review of known sounds in RANDOM order (not chanted in sequence), about 5 minutes
Explicit teaching of the new sound: I do, we do, you do; link sound, letter shape and a key word
Blend the new sound with known sounds into words straight away, every day
Segment spoken words into sounds and spell them with letter cards
Apply in a short decodable text that uses only taught sounds and sight words
Quick individual checks: point to cards out of order and come back to missed ones after two or three others
avoid: Chanting the alphabet or sound charts as the main activity
Predictable picture books that let learners guess instead of decode
Introducing words with sounds not yet taught

frith.looksLike: Recognises familiar words or logos by shape or context only; cannot read the same word in a new font or setting
frith.teach: Phonological awareness, letter-sounds and the alphabetic principle; do not count this as reading

frith.looksLike: Sounds out words letter by letter or syllable by syllable; slow but can read new regular words
frith.teach: Systematic phonics, daily blending and segmenting, decodable texts, then repeated reading

frith.looksLike: Recognises many words instantly and reads with growing speed and expression
frith.teach: Wide reading, fluency with expression, vocabulary and comprehension strategies

simpleView.idea: Reading comprehension depends on both decoding and language comprehension; weakness in either limits reading

profiles.teach: Targeted phonics, blending and decodable texts; read aloud to keep comprehension growing
Oral language, vocabulary, listening comprehension and comprehension strategies
Work on both strands; if progress stalls, refer for further assessment (SIAS)

diagnosticRules.if: A Grade 1 learner sounds fewer than 40 letters correctly in a minute (random order)
diagnosticRules.means: Letter-sound knowledge is not yet strong enough to read words
diagnosticRules.do: Reteach the missed sounds with shuffled-card practice and feedback, then retest

diagnosticRules.if: A learner can recite letters or sounds in order but not when they are mixed up
diagnosticRules.means: The sequence was memorised as a chant; the code itself is not secure
diagnosticRules.do: Replace chanting with random-order card practice to individuals; return to missed cards after two or three others

diagnosticRules.if: A learner reads a two-letter sound (sh, ch, th) as two separate sounds
diagnosticRules.means: Digraphs are not yet known as single units
diagnosticRules.do: Teach each digraph explicitly as one sound, after its single letters, with plenty of word practice

diagnosticRules.if: A learner gives each sound correctly but cannot join them into the word
diagnosticRules.do: Blend daily straight after teaching each sound: build words with letter cards, then read whole words with finger-pointing

diagnosticRules.if: A learner stalls on consonant blends (st, bl, fr) while knowing each letter
diagnosticRules.means: The blend is being treated as a new, unknown sound
diagnosticRules.do: Show the blend as two known sounds said quickly together, then practise in words

diagnosticRules.if: A learner reads familiar real words but fails on made-up (nonsense) words
diagnosticRules.means: Words are being memorised rather than decoded
diagnosticRules.do: More sound–letter and blending practice with decodable lists; real-or-nonsense word games

diagnosticRules.if: A learner reads a picture book well but cannot read the same sentences without pictures
diagnosticRules.means: Reading from picture cues (pictorial stage), not decoding
diagnosticRules.do: Use decodable texts matched to taught sounds instead of predictable picture books

diagnosticRules.if: A learner guesses words from the first letter or the context
diagnosticRules.means: Untaught sounds or weak decoding; guessing quickly becomes a habit
diagnosticRules.do: Give texts that use only taught sounds and prompt the learner to sound out and blend the whole word

diagnosticRules.if: Reading is slow and inaccurate (in English, fewer than about 85% of words correct; in an African home language, fewer than about 95%)
diagnosticRules.means: The problem is decoding accuracy, not speed
diagnosticRules.do: Go back to targeted phonics and word reading before fluency practice

diagnosticRules.if: Reading is accurate (English about 85% or more; African home language about 95% or more) but slow
diagnosticRules.means: Decoding is accurate but not yet automatic
diagnosticRules.do: Repeated reading (up to about four times) of slightly easy texts, plus wide reading; do not push for speed

diagnosticRules.if: Words are read fluently but in a flat, unphrased way
diagnosticRules.do: Model expressive reading in read-alouds and shared reading; teach phrasing and punctuation cues

diagnosticRules.if: A learner reads accurately at a good pace but cannot answer questions
diagnosticRules.means: The gap is in language comprehension (Simple View of Reading)
diagnosticRules.do: Vocabulary, oral language and listening comprehension work; explicit comprehension strategies

diagnosticRules.if: A learner is weak in both decoding and listening comprehension
diagnosticRules.means: Both strands need support; a wider learning difficulty is possible
diagnosticRules.do: Support both strands; if there is no progress, begin the SIAS process for further assessment

diagnosticRules.if: A learner decodes English words but understands little of the text, while understanding more in the home language
diagnosticRules.means: English vocabulary and grammar are the gap, not decoding
diagnosticRules.do: Add English oral language and vocabulary teaching alongside decoding; bridge from the home language

diagnosticRules.if: Most of the class is slow to master letter-sounds
diagnosticRules.means: The phonics pace may be too slow or the teaching too implicit
diagnosticRules.do: Teach explicitly (I do, we do, you do), blend daily and keep a brisk pace: weaker learners benefit most

diagnosticRules.if: A learner cannot say the separate sounds in a short spoken word
diagnosticRules.means: Phonemic awareness (oral) is not yet in place, so letters cannot be linked to sounds
diagnosticRules.do: Oral segmenting and blending games without print (sound buttons, arm tapping), then link each sound to its letter

diagnosticRules.if: A learner reading English as an additional language reads fewer than about 50 correct words per minute
diagnosticRules.means: Reading is still too slow for the learner to understand the text alone (EFAL threshold); comprehension questions on independent reading will mostly fail
diagnosticRules.do: Prioritise decoding and fluency practice for this learner; build comprehension through read-alouds and discussion until reading speed reaches about 50 words per minute

diagnosticRules.if: A Grade 2 learner reading English as an additional language is below about 30 correct words per minute at the end of the year
diagnosticRules.means: The learner is unlikely to reach the Grade 3 threshold of 50 a year later without targeted support
diagnosticRules.do: Add targeted decoding and daily repeated reading now; monitor with a 1-minute reading check each term

africanLanguages.note: For future African home-language versions (MTbBE). Paraphrased from Module 3.
points: Spelling is transparent: letters map consistently to sounds, so decoding can be taught quickly
Most syllables end in a vowel (consonant + vowel); syllables are a natural unit, but learners must still hear the separate sounds inside them
Rhyme does not work well; use repetition, alliteration and reduplication in songs and rhymes instead
Tone and vowel length are not marked in spelling; context decides meaning, so expressive model reading matters

Nguni languages such as isiZulu join morphemes into long words (conjunctive); Sotho languages such as Sesotho write them separately (disjunctive). Long words slow reading, so fluency benchmarks differ by language
Teach two- and three-letter sounds (e.g. hl, kh, tsh) as single units; teach consonant clusters early as sequences of sounds already learned
Morphological awareness (noun prefixes, subject and object morphemes) supports reading long words, incidentally in Grades 1–2 and deliberately in Grade 3

readingActivities.note: Gradual release of responsibility across the five CAPS reading activities (paraphrased from Funda Wande)
order: Teacher read-aloud (teacher reads, learners listen and think)
Shared reading (teacher and learners read an enlarged text together)
Group guided reading (small same-level group reads with the teacher)
Paired reading (learners read with a partner)
Independent reading (learners read on their own)

groupGuidedReading.note: Common South African classroom routine (paraphrased from the DBE/NECT PSRIP lesson plans and Funda Wande)
points: Many classes follow a weekly routine with one group guided reading slot a day, so the teacher reads with each group about once a week
Groups are often formed once, from listening to each learner read in the first weeks of the term
While the teacher reads with one group, the others complete a short reading worksheet that uses only phonic and sight words already taught
Seat a weaker reader next to a stronger reader so that peer support happens during independent work
Learners who finish early choose a book for independent reading
groupGuidedReading.capsDiAdds: CAPS DI regroups learners after every exit task, from the CAPS ratings and error patterns, and tells the teacher which group needs the extra guided-reading slots this week.
